state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: It seems like you're unsure about how changing all the values by the same proportion would affect the range. Let's explore why changing the heights of the plants by the same amount might or might not impact the range. Can you think of a way we could test this idea with the given heights of the plants?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, I guess I could work out the range before and after? So like, the range now is 42 minus 13 which is 29, and then if they all grew by 3 cm it would be 45 minus 16 which is... also 29? Wait, so Katie would be right then? But I thought adding the same amount wouldn't change it...

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: It looks like you're on the right track with comparing the ranges before and after changing the heights. Let's delve deeper into why adding the same amount to each plant might not always affect the range. Can you think of any other scenarios where changing all values by the same proportion would or wouldn't impact the range?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if you add the same amount to both the biggest and smallest plant, the difference between them stays the same... but what about when Tom cuts them all in half? Would that change the range because you're multiplying instead of adding?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher asks open questions but mischaracterizes the mathematical concepts (confusing proportion with addition in Turn 3), and while the student makes progress on addition, they end still uncertain about multiplication, leaving the core misconception about proportional change unresolved.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to break the problem into steps, they fail to adjust support appropriately—the student demonstrates understanding in Turn 2 but the teacher doesn't acknowledge this progress and instead asks a confusing question about 'changing by the same proportion' when the student is actually discussing addition, missing the opportunity to scaffold toward the multiplication aspect the student needs help with.
